title: Spillback host memory slab thresholds and scheduler (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This note collects a cohesive approach for 'spillback' — the runtime behavior where cold KV slots are relocated from GPU-local storage to host memory or NVMe over PCIe — and a lightweight host-side paging/scheduler design that balances tail-latency SLOs and SKU cost. This is a draft for internal review: goal is a pragmatic implementation that can be validated with perf runs and A/B rollout in Dedicated clusters.

Background and motivation:
- Observed behavior: transient working-set growth produces 99th percentile latency spikes when GPU-resident KV pages are evicted or cold-miss fetches hit PCIe NVMe.
- We want deterministic degradation: when local GPU memory pressure grows we should gracefully move cold pages to host rather than thrash or block hot requests.
- Two host topologies to handle: UMA (host and device share coherent memory or fast peer path) and discrete PCIe/NVMe backends. Tradeoffs: UMA gives lower latency but limited capacity; PCIe+NVMe provides capacity at higher per-page latency and throughput variance.

Design goals:
1) Predictable tail: bound 99/99.9p impact by limiting in-flight spillback fetches per model and prioritizing hot page residency.
2) Bounded bandwidth: avoid saturating PCIe/NVMe burst capacity by token-bucket rate-limiting and background flush lanes.
3) Simple integration: scheduler implemented in host control-plane (agent) with hooks into inference path; minimal changes to kernel hot path.
4) Observable and tunable: expose slab thresholds and token counts via Console; autopilot suggestions from Optimize.

Key concepts and components:
- Slab residency classes: HOT (always GPU-resident), WARM (GPU preferred, allowed to be evicted under pressure), COLD (spillback -> host/NVMe). Slots transition by access frequency windows (epoch-based).
- Epoch sampler: per-model lightweight counter that increments on KV hits. Window length default: 1 minute; tunable. Decay multiplier applied every epoch.
- Spillback lanes:
  * Fast lane (UMA peer or NVMe with cached PCIe mappings) — limited parallelism N_fast per GPU.
  * Slow lane (NVMe cold): larger queue, lower concurrency N_slow. Background prefetcher may pull WARM->HOT under idle tail budget.
- Backpressure tokens: a capped token pool per model and per-GPU. A request that needs a spill fetch must acquire a token; if none available, the runtime enqueues request with priority and optionally falls back to a lower-fidelity model variant.

Threshold heuristics (starting defaults for experiments):
- GPU memory pressure threshold -> trigger slab reclassification: 80% used (soft), 92% used (aggressive).
- HOT quota maintained at min(0.6 * available_slots, max_hot_per_model) where max_hot_per_model = 4096 for large-gen models (tunable).
- Token pool sizes: N_fast = 8, N_slow = 32 per GPU. Token refill: steady-state refill 2 tokens/sec for fast lane, 6 tokens/sec for slow lane; burst allowed up to pool cap.
- Epoch sampling: sample window = 60s, decay = 0.75. Promote to HOT if hits > 16 within epoch; demote if hits < 2.

Scheduler pseudocode (host agent):
- on memory pressure event:
    calculate current HOT/WARM/COLD distribution using epoch counts
    target_hot = compute_target_hot_slots()
    mark lowest-score slots as candidates for spillback until hot_slot_count <= target_hot
    enqueue spillback operations into fast/slow lanes based on backend affinity
- on request needing KV page:
    if page in GPU: proceed
    else if obtain_token(page.backend_lane): start fetch and attach token to request
    else: if fallback model available -> route to fallback; else enqueue with priority and return provisional tokens/timeouts

Prefetch/backfill policy:
- During low GPU utilization windows, background agent selects high-score WARM pages for prefetch back to GPU up to a background budget (bg_tokens). Default bg_tokens = 16 per GPU.
- Prefer prefetch for pages observed in consecutive epochs (signal of re-hotting).

Profiling and metrics to collect:
- per-page fetch latency histograms split by lane (UMA/PCIe/NVMe)
- token acquisition wait times
- evictions/sec and spillback throughput
- request tail latency delta attributable to spillback
- background prefetch success ratio

Failure modes and mitigation:
- PCIe burst saturation -> detect via increasing fetch latency and reduce token refill and background prefetch rate automatically.
- Starvation of hot slots due to aggressive prefetch -> cap prefetch to fraction of free slots and prioritize eviction of true COLD pages.
- Torn states (page concurrently moved by two agents) -> use short lease metadata on page descriptor with update CAS via control-plane service to serialize moves.

Open questions and experiments:
1) Right granularity for epoch window vs. per-request recency counters. Lower granularity reduces churn but may delay hotspot promotion.
2) Quantify UMA fast-lane vs PCIe slow-lane thresholds on our hardware matrix (A100 with NVMe, RTX shared nodes). Need microbench: single-page fetch p50/p95/p99, plus throughput at 8/32/128 concurrency.
3) Determine fairness policy cross-tenant: tokens per-tenant or strict per-model pools? Suggest starting with per-model pools with tenant-level debt accounting.
4) Should we expose an opt-in per-customer policy to prefer cost (push more to host) vs prefer latency (reserve extra HOT slots)?

Next steps and rollout plan:
- Implement prototype host-agent token pool + simple spillback enqueuer (3 wk sprint).
- Add observability metrics and synthetic benchmark harness (2 wk).
- Run lab matrix experiments across hardware types to tune N_fast/N_slow and epoch params (2 wk).
- Canary in Dedicated with opt-in SLA toggle and automated rollback on tail-latency regressions (2 wk).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative: token gating allows us to bound worst-case amplification. We should avoid speculative global heuristics until we have per-hardware empirical curves.
- I'm leaving explicit data structures and proto APIs for a follow-up spec — think of this doc as the operational playbook and behavior contract.
